title: Greenhouse Energy & Heat Balance
summary: Protected structures gain, store, and lose heat through solar radiation, glazing, air exchange, equipment, crop transpiration, and outside weather; temperature control is therefore an energy-balance problem, not a thermostat-only problem.
keyConcepts: Solar gain can raise interior temperature rapidly even when outdoor air is mild
Glazing material and structure geometry affect heat gain and loss
Plants and wet surfaces add latent heat and water vapor to the air
Ventilation, shade, evaporative cooling, heating, and dehumidification each change more than one environmental variable
measureObserve: Log inside and outside temperature through the day
Compare sunny and cloudy periods
Identify hot zones near glazing or poor air mixing
Record equipment operation alongside environmental changes
commonMistakes: Treating air temperature as spatially uniform
Adding cooling without checking humidity consequences
Ignoring night heat loss and cold surfaces
Using one sensor as the entire greenhouse
visualNeeds: Solar gain and heat-loss cross section

title: Ventilation, Air Exchange & Circulation
summary: Ventilation replaces greenhouse air with outside air while circulation mixes air inside the structure; both matter, but they solve different problems.
keyConcepts: Air exchange can remove heat and water vapor when outside conditions allow
Horizontal or vertical circulation reduces stagnant zones without necessarily exchanging outside air
Canopy density changes resistance to air movement
Openings, fans, screens, and structure geometry influence airflow patterns
measureObserve: Compare temperature and RH at crop height in several locations
Use lightweight indicators or smoke testing where safe to observe air paths
Inspect dead zones behind dense canopy or structural barriers
Record vent and fan state with sensor data
commonMistakes: Calling circulation fans ventilation
Pointing high-velocity airflow directly at one crop zone
Ignoring blocked intake paths
Assuming fan rating equals delivered airflow through the real structure

title: Humidity, Condensation & Dew-Point Risk
summary: Condensation forms when a surface reaches or falls below the air's dew point. In protected structures, cold glazing, leaves, pipes, and dense flower zones can become wet even when bulk-air RH appears acceptable.
keyConcepts: Relative humidity changes with temperature even when absolute moisture is unchanged
Cold surfaces can reach dew point before room air appears saturated
Night cooling often raises condensation risk
Persistent leaf or flower wetness can increase disease risk
measureObserve: Track temperature and RH overnight
Inspect glazing and crop surfaces near dawn
Compare air temperature with leaf or surface temperature when possible
Note locations where condensation repeatedly forms
commonMistakes: Using daytime RH as the only disease-risk metric
Assuming visible wall condensation is the only meaningful condensation
Heating without considering moisture removal
Dehumidifying one zone while leaving stagnant canopy pockets

title: Greenhouse Sensor Placement & Data Quality
summary: A greenhouse can contain large microclimate differences. Sensor location, shielding, calibration, response time, and maintenance determine whether data describe the crop or merely the sensor's immediate surroundings.
keyConcepts: Radiant heat can bias exposed temperature sensors
Crop-height measurements are often more representative than ceiling measurements
Multiple zones may require multiple sensors
Calibration drift can turn precise-looking numbers into misleading data
measureObserve: Map sensor height and location
Compare two instruments side by side periodically
Shield sensors from direct radiation when appropriate
Review implausible sudden jumps before acting on them
commonMistakes: Mounting the only sensor next to a heater, vent, door, or wet wall
Never checking calibration
Changing controls from one anomalous reading
Assuming dashboard precision equals measurement accuracy

title: Protected-Cultivation Irrigation & Drainage
summary: Protected structures remove rainfall from the crop but do not remove water-management complexity. Irrigation uniformity, substrate storage, drainage, runoff, root oxygen, and crop demand must be tracked together.
keyConcepts: Emitter uniformity can change over time
Drainage fraction alone does not describe root-zone moisture distribution
Protected structures can accumulate salts where natural rainfall never leaches the root zone
Standing water and chronically wet floors can increase humidity and sanitation problems
measureObserve: Catch-test emitters for distribution differences
Inspect moisture at several substrate positions
Track input and representative drainage EC where applicable
Keep floors and drains functioning and observable
commonMistakes: Assuming equal irrigation time means equal delivered volume
Ignoring clogged or displaced emitters
Allowing runoff to pool
Using one container as the only irrigation reference

title: Insect Exclusion Screening & Airflow Tradeoffs
summary: Screens can reduce pest entry, but finer screening also adds resistance to airflow. Exclusion must therefore be designed together with ventilation capacity, pressure, maintenance, and pest size.
keyConcepts: Screen aperture determines which pests can be excluded
Finer mesh generally creates more airflow resistance
Dirty screens progressively reduce airflow
Doors, vents, tears, and service openings can defeat otherwise good screening
measureObserve: Inspect screens for tears and blocked areas
Compare vent performance before and after screen installation
Record temperature rise during peak ventilation demand
Check door and intake pathways for bypass entry
commonMistakes: Selecting the finest mesh without evaluating ventilation penalty
Installing screens but leaving unscreened bypass routes
Failing to clean screens
Assuming screening eliminates the need for scouting

title: Incoming Plant Quarantine & Clean Stock
summary: Incoming clones, plugs, liners, mother stock, and other living material can introduce arthropods and pathogens before obvious symptoms appear. Separation and observation reduce the chance of moving an unseen problem into the main crop.
keyConcepts: Asymptomatic material can still carry pests or pathogens
Vegetative propagation can preserve and spread systemic infections
A physically separated observation area is more useful than a label alone
Records should connect source, date, lot, observations, and disposition
measureObserve: Inspect incoming material under magnification
Check upper and lower leaf surfaces and root zones
Record supplier and lot information
Keep suspect material separated until evidence supports release or removal
commonMistakes: Moving new plants directly into established crops
Relying only on visible leaf symptoms
Sharing tools between quarantine and production without sanitation
Losing lot identity after unpacking

title: Greenhouse Scouting & Hotspot Mapping
summary: Effective greenhouse IPM depends on repeated, mapped observations. Sticky cards, plant inspections, magnification, and records reveal where pest pressure begins and whether it is changing.
keyConcepts: Sticky cards monitor some flying adults but do not replace plant inspection
Pest life stage matters for identification and management timing
Maps make recurring hotspots visible
Scouting should begin when plant material enters the structure
measureObserve: Number and date monitoring cards
Inspect a consistent set of plants or zones
Record eggs, immatures, adults, damage, and beneficial organisms separately
Mark hotspots and revisit them after any intervention
commonMistakes: Counting sticky-card insects without checking plants
Moving traps without recording location
Scouting only after visible damage becomes widespread
Recording presence without abundance or life stage

title: Biological Control Program Design
summary: Biological control works best as a planned IPM component: correctly identify the pest, match a beneficial organism to the pest and life stage, introduce it early enough, and verify establishment through scouting.
keyConcepts: Different beneficial organisms target different pests and life stages
Environmental conditions affect beneficial performance
Preventive or early releases can be more effective than waiting for heavy infestations
Broad-spectrum pesticide residues can disrupt beneficial populations
measureObserve: Confirm pest identity before selecting a biological control
Track beneficial releases by date and location
Scout for both pest and beneficial populations
Review pesticide compatibility before combining tactics
commonMistakes: Releasing a beneficial without confirming the target pest
Expecting immediate knockdown from a population-based biological program
Ignoring temperature and humidity requirements
Using incompatible pesticide residues without checking effects on beneficials

title: High Tunnel vs Greenhouse Environment
summary: High tunnels and actively controlled greenhouses both modify the crop environment, but their ventilation, heating, humidity control, automation, and pest dynamics can differ substantially.
keyConcepts: High tunnels often depend heavily on passive ventilation
Rain exclusion changes leaf wetness and irrigation dependence
Protected environments can favor pest complexes that differ from open-field production
Management decisions must match the actual level of environmental control
measureObserve: Document which controls are active versus passive
Track inside/outside temperature and RH
Record vent-opening patterns and rain exclusion
Compare pest pressure with nearby outdoor crops where relevant
commonMistakes: Applying greenhouse assumptions to a minimally controlled tunnel
Assuming rain exclusion eliminates disease
Ignoring rapid daytime overheating
Treating a protected structure as pest-proof
